newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.S. rating agency team expected to visit Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rating agency team expected to visit Pakistan.

text.p: A U.S. credit rating agency will send analysts to Pakistan next week to review its troubled economy, a local securities firm said on Monday.

Khadim Ali Shah Bukhari & Co Ltd (KASB) said in its daily report that two or three senior rating analysts of Moody's Investors Service Inc would arrive on October 21 to meet State (central) Bank of Pakistan and Finance Ministry officials.
Government officials could not be reached for comment.

Moody's said last month it might cut Pakistan's B1 long-term foreign currency rating and its B2 sovereign ceiling for foreign currency deposits. Pakistan's B1-rated foreign currency bonds and notes were also placed on review for possible downgrade.

The agency had voiced concern at "Pakistan's weakening macroeconomic fundamentals, as evidenced by the deviations from long-standing goals of economic restructuring, as well as increased levels of short-term debt and ongoing balance of payments difficulties".
Analysts said Moody's move would force Pakistan, already paying 1.5-2.0 percentage points above the London Interbank Offered Rate on commercial loans, to pay even higher interest rates.
They said they doubted that a downgrade could be averted unless Pakistan was able to persuade the International Monetary Fund to reactivate a stalled $600 million standby loan.
The IMF has held up disbursements of the standby loan because of doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed reforms and confusion over the 1996/97 (July-June) budget.
Pakistani officials left for Washington on Sunday to discuss a rescue package with the IMF.

Pakistan's donors and lenders remain concerned about the balance of payments, although the trade gap narrowed to $767 million in the first three months of 1996/97 (July-June) from $988 million in the first quarter of 1995/96.
Exports grew 17 percent in July-September, while imports expanded only 2.1 percent, official figures show.

"We remain cautiously optimistic on the market outlook, reserving the call until at least IMF conditions are in place (including possible devaluation) and Moody's review their credit rating," the KASB report said.
